title: Why Cramming Fails: The Science of Spaced Learning
titleCn: 临时抱佛脚为何无效：间隔学习的科学

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every student has tried it: staying up late before an examination, reading the same notes again and again in the hope that the information will still be there the next morning. Sometimes the strategy appears to work, at least for the test itself. But a large body of research suggests that knowledge acquired in this way fades remarkably quickly. Psychologists have known for more than a century that the timing of study matters as much as its total amount, and that the same number of hours can produce very different results depending on how they are distributed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first systematic evidence came from the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, who in the 1880s carried out a long series of experiments on himself. To avoid the influence of meaning, he memorised lists of nonsense syllables, such as combinations of three letters that formed no real word, and then measured how much he could remember after different intervals. He found that forgetting was fastest immediately after learning and then gradually slowed down, a pattern now known as the forgetting curve. He also noticed that lists he reviewed over several days were retained far better than lists he studied for the same total time in a single session.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This advantage of distributed practice, usually called the spacing effect, has since been confirmed in hundreds of studies. It has been demonstrated with children and older adults, with vocabulary, mathematics and motor skills such as typing, and even in animals. One widely cited review of the research concluded that the benefit is among the most reliable findings in the whole of experimental psychology. Typically, people who space their study sessions remember substantially more weeks or months later than those who mass their practice together, even though both groups may perform equally well on a test given immediately afterwards.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why should spacing make such a difference? One explanation focuses on the effort involved in remembering. When information is reviewed while it is still fresh, recalling it is easy, and the brain has little reason to strengthen the memory. When some time has passed and the material has been partly forgotten, retrieving it requires more work, and this struggle appears to make the memory more durable. A second explanation suggests that spaced sessions take place in slightly different situations and moods, so the information becomes linked to a wider range of cues that can later help to bring it back to mind.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Closely related to spacing is what researchers call the testing effect. In a typical experiment, one group of students reads a text several times, while another reads it once and then tries to write down as much as they can remember. On a final test a week later, the second group usually performs better, despite having spent less time looking at the material. The act of retrieval, it seems, is not simply a way of checking what has been learned but a powerful form of learning in itself. Combining the two techniques, by testing oneself at increasing intervals, is often recommended as the most efficient approach of all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Given the strength of the evidence, it is surprising how rarely these methods are used. Surveys of university students show that rereading notes and highlighting textbooks remain the most popular strategies, although both are among the least effective. Part of the reason is that massed study feels more productive. Information that has just been read seems familiar, and this familiarity is easily mistaken for genuine understanding. Spaced practice, in contrast, often feels difficult and slow, and learners may conclude that it is not working at precisely the moment when it is doing most good.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Technology may help to close this gap. Many language-learning applications now use algorithms that schedule reviews automatically, presenting each word just before the learner is likely to forget it and lengthening the interval each time it is recalled correctly. Some schools have also experimented with returning to earlier topics throughout the year rather than teaching each unit only once. Researchers caution that the ideal gap between sessions depends on how long the information needs to be remembered: material required for a test next week should be reviewed differently from knowledge that must last a lifetime.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the length of the working week fell steadily in industrialised countries. Campaigns by trade unions, combined with rising productivity, turned six long days into five shorter ones, and many economists expected the trend to continue. One famous prediction, made in the 1930s, suggested that within a hundred years people might need to work only fifteen hours a week. That forecast now looks wildly optimistic. In many countries the standard week has hardly changed for decades, and in some professions working hours have actually increased.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In recent years, however, the idea of a shorter week has returned to public debate. A number of companies and public bodies have run trials in which staff work four days instead of five, usually for the same pay, on the condition that they maintain their usual output. The organisations involved range from software firms and marketing agencies to restaurants, banks and local councils. In most cases the trial lasts six months, and researchers collect information on productivity, staff well-being and the number of days lost to sickness both before and during the experiment.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The reported results have been striking. Many participating employers say that output stayed the same or even rose, while employees described lower levels of stress and exhaustion and more time for family, exercise and hobbies. Absence through illness often fell, and some firms found it easier to recruit new staff. At the end of these trials, a clear majority of the companies chose to keep the shorter week in some form. To its supporters, this is evidence that much of the traditional working day is wasted in unnecessary meetings, interruptions and tasks that add little value.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Sceptics, however, raise several objections, and in my view some of them deserve more attention than they usually receive. The most important concerns the type of organisation that takes part. Companies volunteer for these trials, and those that do so are likely to be the ones most confident that the change will succeed. Their experience may therefore tell us little about how a four-day week would work in a typical business. In addition, most trials have been too short to show whether early gains last once the novelty has worn off and staff are no longer aware that they are being observed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is also the question of which jobs can be compressed in this way. In an office where work is measured by tasks completed, it may be possible to do in four days what previously took five. In a hospital, a school or a care home, the situation is quite different, because these services must be available every day and their staff cannot simply work faster. Introducing a shorter week in such sectors would require employing more people, which raises costs. It would be a mistake, I believe, to assume that a model which suits a design agency can be applied without change to a nursing team.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters of the idea are not blind to these difficulties. Some argue that the four-day week should be seen not as a single fixed rule but as a general direction, which different sectors could reach in different ways, for example through shorter daily hours or additional days of annual leave. Others point to the possible benefits for society as a whole, including reduced commuting and lower carbon emissions, though these effects have not yet been measured with any precision. A few countries have begun to consider legislation, but so far governments have preferred to encourage experiments rather than to impose change.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: On balance, the evidence so far is encouraging but incomplete. It shows that, for some organisations, working fewer hours need not mean producing less, and that well-being can improve considerably when people have more time away from work. What it does not yet show is that the same results can be achieved across the whole economy. Rather than treating the four-day week as either a cure for modern working life or an impossible dream, policymakers would be wise to support larger and longer trials, particularly in the public services where the challenges are greatest.
